rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

Exposed details about the application’s environment, users, or associated data (for example, stack trace) could enable an attacker to find another flaw and help the attacker to mount an attack. This may also leak sensitive data, e.g. passwords or database fields. 

Cause

How does it happen

The application handles exceptions in an insecure manner, including raw details directly in the error message. This could occur in various ways: by not handling the exception; printing it directly to the output or file; explicitly returning the exception object; or by configuration. These exception details may include sensitive information that could leak to the users due to the occurrence of the runtime error. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Do not expose exception data directly to the output or users, instead return an informative, generic error message. Log the exception details to a dedicated log mechanism.

    • Explicitly handles expected exceptions. 
    • Includes a default solution to explicitly handle unexpected exceptions. 
    • Configure a global handler to prevent unhandled errors from leaving the application.

rule.name: Leaving_Temporary_Files
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

Applications often create temporary files containing sensitive business data or personal information, in order to handle the file generation process in several steps, or even as the output of an automatic process. These files, if left exposed on disk for an indeterminate period of time, could leak the secret data to unauthorized users. 

Cause

How does it happen

It is very common for applications to use temporary files, as intermediate storage and to aid with processing large amounts of data or long-running calculations. Applications require such files so frequently that most operating systems allocate a dedicated area for temporary files, such as a TEMP directory, and several different mechanisms for creating them exist in most platforms. However, by default these temporary files are not deleted automatically, and will remain on disk indefinitely. If the program does not explicitly and proactively delete the temporary files when it is finished processing them, they might be accessbile to other users of the computer. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Always explicitly delete any temporary file created. 
    • Additionally, to ensure that all temporary files will eventually be deleted, consider implementing additional functionality that will periodically scrape and delete all unused, existing temporary files.

rule.name: Leftover_Debug_Code
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

Tests and debugging code are not intended to be deployed to the production environment, and can create unintended entry points, thus increasing the application's attack surface. Furthermore, this code is often not properly tested or maintained, and can retain historic vulnerabilities that were fixed in other parts of the codebase. Often, debug code will contain a functional "back door", by enabling the programmer to bypass operational security mechanisms, such as authentication or access controls. 

Cause

How does it happen

During application development, it is common for programmers to implement specialized code, in order to ease debugging and testing. Often the programmer will even enable the debug code to bypass security mechanisms, so as to focus the tests on the specific functionality and isolate it from the security architecture.  
This debug or test code is not removed from the codebase, and is then included in the software build and deployed to the production environment. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    •  - Remove all debug code before deploying or building the application. Ensure the configuration settings are not defined to enable debug mode.  
    •  - Implement all test code via a dedicated test framework, which can isolate the test case code from the rest of the application.  
    •  - Avoid implementing special "test code", "debugging-time" functionality, or "secret" interfaces or parameters in the application code itself.  
    •  - Define and implement a standard and automatic build / deployment process, using dedicated CI / CD tools, that can automatically configure the deployed application, exclude all temporary code, and include only intended application code. 

]]

rule.name: Log_Forging
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

An attacker could engineer audit logs of security-sensitive actions and lay a false audit trail, potentially implicating an innocent user or hiding an incident. 

Cause

How does it happen

The application writes audit logs upon security-sensitive actions. Since the audit log includes user input that is neither checked for data type validity nor subsequently sanitized, the input could contain false information made to look like legitimate audit log data, 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • 1. Validate all input, regardless of source. Validation should be based on a whitelist: accept only data fitting a specified structure, rather than reject bad patterns. Check for: 
    • Data type 
    • Size 
    • Range 
    • Format 
    • Expected values 
    • 3. Validation is not a replacement for encoding. Fully encode all dynamic data, regardless of source, before embedding it in logs. 
    • 4. Use a secure logging mechanism. 

]]

rule.name: NULL_Pointer_Dereference
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

A null pointer dereference is likely to cause a run-time exception, a crash, or other unexpected behavior. 

Cause

How does it happen

Variables which are declared without being assigned will implicitly retain a null value until they are assigned. The null value can also be explicitly set to a variable, to ensure clear out its contents. Since null is not really a value, it may not have object variables and methods, and any attempt to access contents of a null object, instead of verifying it is set beforehand, will result in a null pointer dereference exception. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • For any variable that is created, ensure all logic flows between declaration and use assign a non-null value to the variable first. 
    • Enforce null checks on any received variable or object before it is dereferenced, to ensure it does not contain a null assigned to it elsewhere. 
    • Consider the need to assign null values in order to overwrite initialized variables. Consider reassigning or releasing these variables instead. 

]]

rule.name: Potential_Path_Traversal
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

An attacker could define arbitrary file path for the application to use, potentially leading to: 
* Stealing sensitive files, such as configuration or system files* Overwriting files such as program binaries, configuration files, or system files* Deleting critical files, causing denial of service (DoS). 

Cause

How does it happen

The application uses user input in the file path for accessing files on the application server’s local disk. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • 1. Ideally, avoid depending on dynamic data for file selection. 
    • 2. Validate all input, regardless of source. Validation should be based on a whitelist: accept only data fitting a specified structure, rather than reject bad patterns. Check for: 
    • Data type 
    • Size 
    • Range 
    • Format 
    • Expected values 
    • 4. Accept dynamic data only for the filename, not for the path and folders. 
    • 5. Ensure that file path is fully canonicalized. 
    • 6. Explicitly limit the application to use a designated folder that is separate from the applications binary folder. 
    • 7. Restrict the privileges of the application’s OS user to necessary files and folders. The application should not be able to write to the application binary folder, and should not read anything outside of the application folder and data folder. 

]]

rule.name: Race_Condition_In_Cross_Functionality
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

At best, a Race Condition may cause errors in accuracy, overidden values or unexpected behavior that may result in denial-of-service. At worst, it may allow attackers to retrieve data or bypass security processes by replaying a controllable Race Condition until it plays out in their favor. 

Cause

How does it happen

Race Conditions occur when a public, single instance of a resource is used by multiple concurrent logical processes. If the these logical processes attempt to retrieve and update the resource without a timely management system, such as a lock, a Race Condition will occur. 
An example for when a Race Condition occurs is a resource that may return a certain value to a process for further editing, and then updated by a second process, resulting in the original process' data no longer being valid. Once the original process edits and updates the incorrect value back into the resource, the second process' update has been overwritten and lost. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • When sharing resources between concurrent processes across the application ensure that these resources are either thread-safe, or implement a locking mechanism to ensure expected concurrent activity. 

]]

rule.name: Stored_Blind_SQL_Injections
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

An attacker could directly access all of the system's data. The attacker would be able to steal any sensitive information stored by the system (such as personal user details or credit cards), and possibly change or erase existing data. 

Cause

How does it happen

The application communicates with its database by sending a textual SQL query. The application creates the query by simply concatenating strings including data obtained from the database. Since that data may have been previously obtained from user input, and is neither checked for data type validity nor subsequently sanitized, the data could contain SQL commands that would be interpreted as such by the database. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • 1. Validate all data, regardless of source. Validation should be based on a whitelist: accept only data fitting a specified structure, rather than reject bad patterns. Check for: 
    • Data type 
    • Size 
    • Range 
    • Format 
    • Expected values 
    • 3. Instead of concatenating strings: 
    • Use secure database components such as stored procedures, parameterized queries, and object bindings (for commands and parameters). 
    • An even better solution is to use an ORM library, such as EntityFramework, Hibernate, or iBatis. 
    • 4. Restrict access to database objects and functionality, according to the Principle of Least Privilege. 

]]

A program that does not check function return values could cause the application to enter an undefined state. This could lead to unexpected behavior and unintended consequences, including inconsistent data, system crashes or other error-based exploits.

rule.name: Use_Of_Deprecated_Class
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

Referencing deprecated modules can cause an application to be exposed to known vulnerabilities, that have been publicly reported and already fixed. A common attack technique is to scan applications for these known vulnerabilities, and then exploit the application through these deprecated versions. However, even if deprecated code is used in a way that is completely secure, its very use and inclusion in the code base would encourage developers to re-use the deprecated element in the future, potentially leaving the application vulnerable to attack, which is why deprecated code should be eliminated from the code-base as a matter of practice. 
Note that the actual risk involved depends on the specifics of any known vulnerabilities in older versions. 

Cause

How does it happen

The application references code elements that have been declared as deprecated. This could include classes, functions, methods, properties, modules, or obsolete library versions that are either out of date by version, or have been entirely deprecated. It is likely that the code that references the obsolete element was developed before it was declared as obsolete, and in the meantime the referenced code was updated. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Always prefer to use the most updated versions of libraries, packages, and other dependancies. 
    • Do not use or reference any class, method, function, property, or other element that has been declared deprecated. 

]]

rule.name: Use_of_Insufficiently_Random_Values
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

Random values are often used as a mechanism to prevent malicious users from knowing or predicting a given value, such as a password, encryption key, or session identifier. Depending on what this random value is used for, an attacker would be able to predict the next numbers generated, or previously generated values, based on sources often used to derive certain randomness; however, while they may seem random, large statistical samples would demonstrate that they are insufficiently random, producing a much smaller space of possible "random" values than a truly random sample would. This could enable an attacker to derive or guess this value, and thus hijack another user's session, impersonate another user, or crack an encryption key (depending on what the pseudo-random value was used for). 

Cause

How does it happen

The application uses a weak method of generating pseudo-random values, such that other numbers could be determined from a relatively small sample size. Since the pseudo-random number generator used is designed for statistically uniform distribution of values, it is approximately deterministic. Thus, after collecting a few generated values, it would be possible for an attacker to calculate past or future values. Specifically, if this pseudo-random value is used in any security context, such as one-time passwords, keys, secret identifiers or salts - an attacker would likely be able to predict the next value generated and steal it, or guess a previously generated value and spoof its original intent. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Always use a cryptographically secure pseudo-random number generator, instead of basic random methods, particularly when dealing with a security context 
    • Use the cryptorandom generator that is built-in to your language or platform, and ensure it is securely seeded. Do not seed the generator with a weak, non-random seed. (In most cases, the default is securely random).  
    • Ensure you use a long enough random value, thus making brute-force attacks unfeasible. 

]]

rule.name: Use_of_Sizeof_On_a_Pointer_Type
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

Using sizeof on a pointer will always return the size of a pointer in the current architecture, resulting in incorrect arithmetic when this value is later used. If it is used as part of a length check, the application may experience unexpected behavior. If it is used to calculate memory allocation, it may result in a buffer overflow. 

Cause

How does it happen

Calculating the size of a pointer, instead of the size of the value it is pointing to, will return a constant number that is the size of a pointer. While this is the correct way to measure the size of a word on current architecture, this issue may be the result of incorrect memory size checks that would lead to miscalculations. 
In C and C++, this confusion often occurs when an array is passed to a function, at which point its size is that of a pointer, because arrays are reduced to pointers to the start of an array, rather than its length. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Ensure objects are correctly passed to sizeof checks, rather than their pointers. 
    • When passing arrays to a function, do not rely on sizeof inside the function, as the array has been reduced to a pointer to the beginning of the array 

]]

rule.name: R01_04_Emergent_Features_Shall_Not_Be_Used
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

There may be instances of undefined, undetermined, or implementation-defined behavior connected to the use of the language features prohibited by this rule. 

Cause

How does it happen

New language capabilities offered by updates to the C Standard have proven helpful in the implementation of more flexible and complicated solutions. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • This rule prohibits the use of all of these novel features and requires that any such use be accompanied by a deviation to guarantee that any undesirable behaviors are recognized and measures are put in place to prevent them from jeopardizing safety or security. 

]]

rule.name: R02_X_Unused_Code
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

Rule 2.1: Some statements and expressions move control flow out of the current code block. Any statements that come after such a jump or function call are unreachable, and either this dead code should be removed, or the logic should be corrected. 
Rule 2.2: Dead code is defined as any operation whose result does not affect the behavior of the program. The presence of dead code indicates that a logic error has occurred as a result of changes to a program or the programs environment. Dead code is usually optimized out of a program during compilation. However, to improve readability and ensure that logic errors are resolved, dead code should be identified and removed from the code. 
Rule 2.4: When a tag is declared but not used in the code, it can cause misunderstanding problems on the part of the programmer to define if the tag was declared redundantly or should not be present in the code. To improve the quality of the code and ensure that declarations mistakes are solved, unused tags should be identified and removed from the code. 
Rule 2.6: Labels that are declared and not used anywhere in the code are most likely to cause an error during program execution. Unused labels should be identified and removed from the code. 
Rule 2.7: Parameters not used in functions can cause misunderstandings problems on the part of the programmer. Whatever values are passed to the unused parameters, the behavior will be the same. It is possible to have an unused parameter because the function needs to have a fixed prototype model, but this type of occurrence must be avoided and parameters not used in functions must be removed from the code. 

Cause

How does it happen

- For 2.1:Code after the use of expression or statements that moves the control flow out of current code block. 
- For 2.2: 
Use of unassigned cast expressions in the body of the statement, unassigned operations involving binary operators), call of empty methods and dead +, -, * and / operators (add by 0, subtract by 0, multiply by 1 and divide by 1). 
- For 2.4: 
When a tag is declared but not used in the scope/code block. 
- For 2.6: 
When a label is declared but not used in the scope/code block. 
- For 2.7: 
When a declared function has unused parameters in its definition. (parameters not used in the function body). 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Be careful not to use expressions or statements that move the flow of control out of the current code block when there is still code to be executed after these statements. 
    • When changing a variable, whether by arithmetic operation, side effect or reference, always assign this modification to another variable. 
    • Do not add by 0, subtract by 0, multiply by 1 and divide by 1 in the code. 
    • Make sure to declare labels, tags and function parameters that will certainly be used in the code. 

]]

rule.name: R03_X_Comments
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

The way comments are written can cause reading confusions and, in some situations, lead to code lines to get ignored. 

Cause

How does it happen

The use of comment markup inside other comments, or the use of line splice in comments. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Do not use /* inside comments (single line or multiline comments) 
    • Do not use '//' inside multiline comments 
    • Do not end single line comments with a backslash (line splice) 

]]

rule.name: R04_X_Character_Sets
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

There is potential for confusion due difficulty of reading strings with both cases. 

Cause

How does it happen

Difficulty of reading strings with both cases, either because it looks like lack of information, or because of confusion with other kind of expressions. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Octal and hexadecimal escape sequences must be terminated by one of the following: 
    • The start of another escape sequence; 
    • The end of the character constant; 
    • The end of the string literal; 
    • Do not use trigraphs; 

]]

rule.name: R05_X_Identifiers
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

- Inner scope identifiers may hide outer scope identifiers, leading to developers confusion;- If identifiers are not distinct (i.e. then only differ in non-significant characters), the system behaviour is undefined;- Long identifiers may reduce code readability; 

Cause

How does it happen

- Some coding patterns (for example, naming "stacking") may produce long identifiers;- Coding bad practices lead to inner scope identifiers equal to outer scope identifiers;- Some automatic code generator systems may produce long identifiers; 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Keep identifiers length below the C implementation limit (63, in C99); 
    • Do not use inner scope identifiers with same name of outer scope identifiers; 
    • Try to customize the automatic code generator systems to avoid long identifiers; 

]]

rule.name: R06_X_Bitfields
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

Depending on the compiler, plain int bitfield declaration may have different ranges of values. To avoid potential errors, it is strictly necessary to specify the signedness of these variables (signed or unsigned). 
In case of single-bit bitfield, the values that can be represented by a signed bitfield with a length of one bit may not meet programmers expectations. According to the C99 Standard, Section 6.2.6.2, a single-bit signed bitfield has a one sign bit and no value bits. 
- Exceptions 
1. The use of enum, short, char or any other type of bitfield is not allowed in C90.2. Base type bool is a exception to the Rule 6.11. The Rule 6.2 does not apply to unnamed bitfields because their values cannot be accessed. 
- Limitations 
1. Detection of typedefs to designate an appropriate type is not considered on this query. 

Cause

How does it happen

When programmers declare bitfields in the code: 
- With no explicitly defined signed int or unsigned int base types.- A single-bit bitfield using signed signedness. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Always declare bitfields defining the signedness (signed int or unsigned int). 
    • Do not declare signed single-bit bitfield. 
    • Avoid using of unnamed bitfields, since their values cannot be accessed. 

]]

rule.name: R07_01_Octal_Constans_Shall_Not_Be_Used
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

Developers writing octal constants may mistakenly not recognize them, expecting that these octal constants be interpreted as decimal constants. 
- Exceptions 
1. The integer constant zero ( 0 ), is understood as an octal constant, but it is an exception to this rule. 
2. This rule does not apply to octal escape sequences (backslash followed by octal digits). 

Cause

How does it happen

The use of octal literals can make code difficult to read, especially when skimming through it. Misinterpreting of numeric values may result in various errors in the code and faults of programming logic. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Do not use octal constants in the code. 
    • Check the real need to use octal constants instead of decimal constants. 
    • If it is strictly necessary, use octal escape sequences instead of writing octal constants with a leading zero. 

]]

rule.name: R07_02_U_Or_u_Suffix_Shall_Be_Applied_To_All_Unsigned_Type_Integers
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

Developers declaring unsigned type integers in the code with no "U" or "u" suffix may mistakenly not recognize them, causing misunderstandings in code analysis and programming errors depending on the environment used. 
- Exceptions 
1. All unsuffixed (with no "U" or "u" suffix) decimal value less than 2147483648 is considered signed. 

Cause

How does it happen

When programmers declare unsigned type decimals, octals and hexadecimals in the code with no "U" or "u" suffix. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Always declare unsigned type constants with "U" or "u". Makes it clear to the programmer that these variables are of unsigned type. 
    • Do not use "U or "u" suffix in signed type constants. 
    • Remember that all unsuffixed decimal value less than 2147483648 is considered signed. 

]]

rule.name: R07_03_Lowercase_l_Shall_Not_Be_Used_In_A_Literal_Suffix
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

Developers declaring long or long long type variables in the code using the lowercase "l" suffix may get confused during code analysis, since the lowercase "l" character can be easily misinterpreted as a decimal "1". 
- Exceptions 
There are no exceptions to this rule 
- Coverage 
1. Reals, decimals, octals and hexadecimals constants. 

Cause

How does it happen

When programmers declare decimals, octals and hexadecimals in the code with lowercase "l" suffix. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Always declare reals, decimals, octals and hexadecimals long type constants with uppercase "L". Makes it clear to the programmer that this suffix is ​​unambiguous 
    • In case of long long type constants, use uppercase "LL" suffix. 
    • When unsigned long or unsigned long long type constants, use uppercase "ULL" or "LLU" suffixes. 

]]

rule.name: R07_04_String_Literal_Should_Be_Assigned_To_Pointer_To_Const_Char
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

The behavior is undefined if a program attempts to modify any portion of a string literal. Modifying a string literal frequently results in an access violation because string literals are typically stored in read-only memory. 
Avoid assigning a string literal to a pointer to non-const or casting a string literal to a pointer to non-const. A pointer to (or array of) const characters must be treated as a string literal. 

Cause

How does it happen

When programmers assign string literals in char base type defined in the code. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Always assign string literals to a pointer to const-qualified char in the code. Makes it clear to the programmer that if this condition is violated, it can cause undefined behavior on the code. 

]]

rule.name: R08_02_Function_Prototype_With_Named_Parameters
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

Structural differences between functions definitions and their invokes may lead to undefined behaviours. 

Cause

How does it happen

The C90 standard introduced function prototypes, but neither C90 nor C99 require the use of function prototypes due backward compatibility. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • When writing function prototypes add a name to each parameter. 
    • *Note**: An empty parameter list is not valid declaration, If a function has no parameters, its prototype must use the keyword _void_. 

]]

rule.name: R08_03_Functions_Have_Same_Name
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

Inconsistent names and typing may cause certain classes of programming errors. First, the names and types of each declaration are syntactic attributes, which may be understood just by looking at the program rather than running it. Second, a variable may only be used in ways that are consistent with its type — for example, double operations on an int value are wrong (the int value must first be cast to double format). 

Cause

How does it happen

C does not require the names of function declarations and their definitions to be the same. But if they, for example, have different types it will allow for inconsistent behavior of the function invocation. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Specify parameter names in function prototypes. 
    • Always use the same names types and type qualifiers for both the declarations and definitions of a function or object. 

]]

rule.name: R08_04_Compatible_Declaration_Shall_Be_Visible
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

Mismatch between objects and functions definitions and their invocations may lead to undefined behaviours. 

Cause

How does it happen

The C90 standard introduced object declarations and function prototypes, but neither C90 nor C99 require the use of them due backward compatibility. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Always use objects declarations and function prototypes, preferably putting them in header files. 

]]

rule.name: R08_05_External_Objects_Shall_Be_Declared_Once
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

The lack of consistency between objects and functions declarations and their definitions, or different declarations of the same object or function, may lead to undefined behaviours. 

Cause

How does it happen

The C90 standard introduced object declarations and function prototypes, but neither C90 nor C99 require the use of them due backward compatibility. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Always use objects declarations and function prototypes, putting them in header files, and include those header files in any translation unit in which the identifiers are defined or used. 

]]

rule.name: R08_06_Single_External_Definition_Per_External_Identifier
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

If an identifier is used for which there are numerous definitions (in various files) or no definition at all, the behavior is uncertain. 

Cause

How does it happen

This issue is caused by different external definitions of the same external identifier. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Do not define the same external identifier in different files, even if the definitions are the same. 

]]

rule.name: R08_07_Function_And_Objects_Should_Not_Use_Extern_When_Referenced_In_One_File
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

When there is no visibility restriction, objects can be used and functions can be called inadvertently, causing confusion to the programmer and problems in understanding the code. 

Cause

How does it happen

When programmers declare objects and/or functions with external definition and these are used in only a single file in addition to the header file or definition file. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Avoid using the extern definition in objects and functions that will be used in only one file. Makes the scope of use of objects and/or functions clear to the programmer. 

]]

rule.name: R08_08_Static_Shall_Be_Used_In_All_Internal_Linkage_Declarations
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

As the C99 Standard declares that if more than one declaration of an object or function are visible in a single translation unit, the linkage assumed is of the earliest declaration, this can lead to confusion if _extern_ and _static_ declarations for the same object or function exist in the same translation unit. 

Cause

How does it happen

The lack of consistent storage class specifier requirement in the C99 Standard. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • The _static_ storage class specifier shall be applied to objects and functions with internal linkage. 

]]

rule.name: R08_09_Identifiers_Should_Be_Defined_At_Block_Scope
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

When an object is defined at block scope, it decreases the chance of it being accessible mistakenly 

Cause

How does it happen

Objects might be defined at global scope in order to be accessible from different scopes. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Only define an object identifier at global scope when it is used by more than one function. However, there are situations in which it may not comply with this rule and, in these situations, some projects may prefer not to apply this rule. 

]]

rule.name: R08_10_Inline_Function_Shall_Be_Declared_With_Static
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

If a function is declared with an inline function specifier, then the function shall be defined in the same translation unit. If this premise is not followed, the application behavior for this condition is undefined and may vary from compiler to compiler. 
To ensure that each instance of function defined as inline is treated as a separate function, it is strictly necessary to use the static specifier in the function definition in each translation unit. 

Cause

How does it happen

When programmers declare functions using inline as a specifier without static storage class specifier. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Do not declare functions using inline specifier without static storage class specifier already defined in the beginning of the function. 

]]

rule.name: R08_11_Extern_Array_Shall_Be_Declared_With_Determined_Size
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

When an extern array is declared without a previously defined size, it can cause misinterpretation problems for the programmer, making it necessary to analyze large parts of the code in search of the limits of the array. 
It is safer to previously define the size of the array, making it easier to check the consistency of the declaration. 

Cause

How does it happen

When programmers declare extern array with unspecified size. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Do not declare extern arrays without a previously defined size. It is strictly necessary to set array boundaries when there is external linkage. 

]]

rule.name: R08_12_Value_Implicitly_Specified_Of_Enumeration_Constant_Shall_Be_Unique
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

When an enumerator list is provided with no explicit initialization enum constants, the C language will allocate a sequence of integers starting at zero for the first element and increasing by one for each subsequent element. 
Explicit initialization of enum constants in the enumerator list, which is also allowed, avoids the mixing of automatic and manual allocation, which is error prone. 

Cause

How does it happen

When programmers declare an enumerator list with no explicit initialization of enum constants. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • To avoid memory allocation and misunderstanding errors, always explicitly initialize all enum constants that have non-unique values 

]]

rule.name: R08_13_Pointer_Should_Point_Const
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

Any non const-qualified parameter may be inadvertently modified in a function. 

Cause

How does it happen

Lack of const-qualified types in parameters. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Whenever it is possible, use pointers that point to const-qualified types. 

]]

rule.name: R08_14_Restrict_Type_Qualifier
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

If restrict is used incorrectly, there is a high risk that the compiler may produce code that does not perform as intended. 

Cause

How does it happen

When used correctly, the restrict type qualifier can help a compiler write more efficient code. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • The programmer must ensure that two or more pointers do not operate on the same memory location. 

]]

rule.name: R09_01_Value_Not_Read_Before_Being_Set
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

The C programming language Standard specifies that objects with static duration are initialized to zero, but for the others, initialization depends on the compiler, and thus, its value is unpredictable. 

Cause

How does it happen

Programmers not initializing variables, and allowing the possibility for them to be accessed prior to value storage. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Programmers should guarantee the initialization of variables. 

]]

rule.name: R09_02_to_03_Array_Initializer_Validation
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

Explicit initialization of each element in the array ensures that all items have been assigned the expected value. The use of braces in the initialization provides clarity to the programmer when initializing large and complex arrays. 
- Exceptions 
1. It is possible to use form { 0 } to initialize an array. This indicates that all elements will be initialized with zero (Rule 9.2 and 9.3). 
2. The array can be initialized using string (Rule 9.2). 
3. The array initialized with a single string literal does not require explicit initializer for each element (Rule 9.3). 
4. Arrays can be partially initialize when designated-initializers are used (Rule 9.2 and 9.3). 

Cause

How does it happen

When programmers declare array partially initialized and do not use braces as initialization separators. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • If one or more array elements are initialized explicitly, it is mandatory to explicitly initialized all the other elements in the array. Makes it clear to the programmer that all items have been assigned the expected value. 
    • Using braces separators when initializing arrays and subarrays makes it clear to the programmer that all indices have been initialized correctly. 

]]

rule.name: R10_01_Operands_Shall_Not_Be_Of_An_Inappropriate_Essential_Type
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

When the data types of the operands are restricted according to the operator used, conversion problems and overflows can occur and cause misunderstandings problems to the programmers. 
- Exceptions: 
1. Non-negative constant expression of signed type may be use as the right operand to a shift operator. 

Cause

How does it happen

When operators are used in certain database types described below: 
Operator: [ ]Essential type restriction to the operands: boolean, character and floating 
Operator: unary +Essential type restriction to the operand: boolean, character and enum 
Operator: unary -Essential type restriction to the operand: boolean, character, enum and unsigned 
Operator: + and -Essential type restriction to the operands: boolean and enum 
Operator: * and /Essential type restriction to the operands: boolean, character and enum 
Operator: %Essential type restriction to the operands: boolean, character, enum and floating 
Operator: < > <= >=Essential type restriction to the operands: boolean 
Operator: == !=Essential type restriction to the operands: No restriction 
Operator: ! && ||Essential type restriction to the operands: character, enum, signed, unsigned and floating 
Operator: << >>Essential type restriction to the operands: boolean, character, enum, signed and floating 
Operator: ~ & | ^Essential type restriction to the operands: boolean, character, enum, signed and floating 
Operator: ? : (1st operand)Essential type restriction to the operands: character, enum, signed, unsigned and floating 
Operator: ? : (2nd and 3rd operands)Essential type restriction to the operands: No restriction 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Avoid using the restricted base types of each type of operator, preventing failures and misunderstanding problems. 

]]

rule.name: R10_02_Char_Type_Shall_Not_Be_Used_Inappropriately_In_Operations
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

When expressions of essential character type are used in addition and subtract operations, conversions problems can occur and causing code misinterpretation to the programmers. 

Cause

How does it happen

When essential character types are use in addition and subtract operations, these statements described below will cause rule violations: 
1. Subtract expressions that have non-char on the left side and non char, non-signed-unsigned on the right side2. Subtract expressions that have char on the both sides assigned to non-int variable3. Subtract expressions that have char on the left side and signed-unsigned on the right side assigned to non-int variable4. Subtract expressions that have signed-unsigned on the left side and char on the right side assigned to non-char variable5. Addition expressions that have non-char, non-signed-unsigned on the both sides6. Addition expressions that have char on the both sides7. Addition expressions that have signed-unsigned on the left side and char on the right side8. Addition expressions that have char on the left side and signed-unsigned on the right side assigned to non-char variable 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Avoid break the statements described on "Cause" topic. Makes it clear to the programmer that conversions problems will not occur. 

]]

rule.name: R10_03_Value_Of_An_Expression_Assigned_To_Inappropriate_Essential_Type
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

When the value of an expression is assigned to inappropriate essential type, hidden problems such as loss of sign, value, or precision can occur and cause misunderstandings problems to the programmers. 
- Exceptions 
1. Value { 0 } can be used to initialize aggregate types.2. Signed int can be assigned to an object of type unsigned int if it value can be represented in that type 

Cause

How does it happen

When the value of an expression is assigned to a narrower essential type or different essential type category. Literals out-of-range assigned to some essentials type is also considered restricted. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • 1. Do not assign expressions to a narrower essential type or different essential type category, preventing failures and misunderstanding problems. 

]]

rule.name: R10_04_Binary_Operator_Operands_With_Same_Type
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

The usage of different fundamental types on binary operators may incur data loss. 

Cause

How does it happen

The use of different operand fundamental types in operations. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Operands for every binary operator should have the same fundamental type. Whenever that is not possible, an explicit cast should be used. 

]]

rule.name: R10_05_Value_Of_An_Expression_Cast_To_Inappropriate_Essential_Type
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

Type casting from one essential type to another may be dangerous or meaningless. In most of cases, this will result in unspecified behavior. 
The casts described below should be avoided: 
- Type casting from bool to any other type;- Type casting from char to bool, enum and floating;- Type casting from enum to bool and enum;- Type casting from signed/unsigned integer to bool and enum;- Type casting from floating to bool, char and enum; 
- Exceptions 
1. Values 0 and 1 may be cast to a essential type boolean, according to the non-C99 boolean implementation. 

Cause

How does it happen

When the value of an expression is cast to inappropriate essential type, according to the constraint list on the "Risk" topic. Values ​​0 and 1 have special exception when used as cast to bool. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Avoid using type casting in type conversions when the conversion is described in the constraint list. 
    • It is considered good programming practice to use the cast operator whenever type conversions are required. However, It is necessary to be careful to not convert to a restricted type, causing a dangerous situation. 

]]

rule.name: R10_06_to_08_Composite_Expressions
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

Unintended results from numeric calculations. 

Cause

How does it happen

The result type (and size) of any numeric calculations depends on the implementation of numeric types, and the architecture (32-bits or 64-bits). 
When working with composite expressions, the result type depends on the type of the operands and not the assigned object type. After any integer promotion, or operand casting, the type of the operands may change. 
Composite expressions are those that have composite operators, as following: 
- Multiplicatives (*, /, %) 
- Additives (binary +, binary -) 
- Bitwise (&, |, ^, ~) 
- Shift (<<, >>) 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Whenever using composite expressions, use operands with the same essential type. 

]]

rule.name: R11_X_Pointer_Type_Conversions
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

Most of the time, pointer conversions that are not permitted by the standard result in undefined behavior. 

Cause

How does it happen

Pointer types give more flexibility in working with complex types but because the language is more flexible on this matter there is a significant risk of writing code with undefined behavior. 
According to MISRA C:2012, the only conversions between pointers permitted by the standard are: 
- From a pointer type into void;- From a pointer type into an arithmetic type;- From an arithmetic type into a pointer type;- From one pointer type into another pointer type. 
Some pointer type conversions also require an explicit cast expression. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • For pointer type conversions without explicit cast some recommendations are: 
    • Do not perform a conversion between a pointer to a function and any other type; 
    • Do not use incomplete types in pointer type conversions; 
    • Do not perform pointer conversions between pointers to objects and integer types; 
    • Do not convert a pointer to void into a pointer to object; 
    • Use only macro NULL for null pointer constants. 
    • While for conversions with explicit cast expressions: 
    • Do not convert pointers to different object types; 
    • Do not perform casts between pointers to void and arithmetic types. 

]]

rule.name: R12_01_Explicit_Operator_Precedence
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

Unexplicit operator precedence may lead the programmers to commit mistakes or interpret the code wrong. 

Cause

How does it happen

The C language features a sizable number of operators, many of which lack obvious relative precedence. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • There is a reduced chance that the programmer's expectations are off when operator precedence is made explicit with parentheses. 

]]

rule.name: R12_02_Right_Operand_Of_Shift_Operator_Out_Of_Range
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

When using negative right hand operand or greater than/equal to the bits width of the left hand operand, an undefined behavior can occur, causing the program to work incorrectly and causing misunderstandings on the part of the programmer. 

Cause

How does it happen

- Use of negative integer literal in the right hand operand of shift operator. 
- If a number or variable is shifted more than the size of the variable on the left side of the shift operator. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Do not use negative integer literal in the right hand operand of shift operator. 
    • Avoid using shift operators in negative numbers. Makes it clear to the programmer the range of the variable. 
    • Make sure the size of the variable in bits on which you want to perform the shift operation. For large bit shift, use unsigned long or unsigned long long variable data types. 

]]

rule.name: R12_03_Comma_Operator_Shall_Not_Be_Used
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

The use of comma operator can lead the programmer to misunderstand the code. 

Cause

How does it happen

As the comma operator has the lowest precedence of any C operator, and acts as a sequence point, it can be hard to understand and interpret some source code pieces. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Don't use comma operator. Rather, use block constructions or similar. 

]]

rule.name: R12_04_Unsigned_Integer_Wrap_Around
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

The constant unsigned integer expressions that wrap-around are not detected by the compiler and may cause an undesired effect during program execution. 

Cause

How does it happen

Wrap-around occurs when trying to represent a very small (negative) or very large (larger than the type can represent) value in an unsigned type variable. Via modular arithmetic, wrap-around reduces the value to the modulus of the types bitwidth. It is a well-defined behavior in standard C. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Make sure that in constant expressions involving arithmetic operations, the operands used and the result of the expression will not overflow the maximum or minimum value allowed for the data type. 
    • It is important to be aware of which architecture is being used (16, 32 or 64 bits) to ensure that the evaluation of a constant expressions will not result in a wrap-around. 
    • Prefer to use macros to control the maximum values of each type of data depending on each architecture. 

]]

rule.name: R12_05_Sizeof_Operand_Not_Array_Of_Type
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

Inappropriate calculation, if based on arrays passed by parameter. 

Cause

How does it happen

According to C Standard, if an __array of type__ is declarated as a function parameter, it _degenerates_ to __pointer to type__. So, any _sizeof_ operator that uses an __array of type__ passed by parameter as operand will return the __type pointer size__, instead of the __array size__. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Do not use __array of type__ as operand of sizeof operator, if the array is a function parameter. 

]]

rule.name: R13_X_Side_Effects
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

When using persistent side effects in initializer list, it can cause an undefined behavior. Initializers are executed in an unspecified order, the result of a conflict is potentially as damaging for the application. 
The same can occur in full expressions or in expressions between sequence points. Expressions and its persistent side effects can be sensitive to evaluation order and compiler-dependent. These kind of expressions are considered unsafe code. 
Expressions with multiple side effects can be confusing to programmers reading or maintaining the code. These problems can occur with increment and decrement operators that can be applied to or after the expression evaluation, and with the assignment operator "=", that can easily be mistaken for equality. 
The Rule 13.5 restricts the use of side effects in operators && and ||, in order to reduce misunderstandings on the part of the programmer, thinking that the side effect will always occur when in fact it is only performed conditionally. 
About the restriction defined in rule 13.6, the operand of sizeof is evaluated only in rare situations, and only according to C99 rules, which can make an undefined behavior. 

Cause

How does it happen

For rule 13.1:- Use of persistent side effects in initialisers (array or expression initialization) 
For rule 13.2:- Perform read/modification access in a volatile-type variable more than once in a full expression or between sequence points. 
For rule 13.3:- Use of multiple side effects in the same expression 
For rule 13.4:- Use the result of assignment in expressions 
For rule 13.5:- When the right-hand operand of && and || operators contains persistent side effects 
For rule 13.6:- Use of persistent side effects in sizeof operand 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Avoid using persistent and non-persistent side effects in initializers. 
    • Always perform increment and decrement operations before or right after assigning it to a variable. 
    • Avoid using multiple side effects or in combination with other operators in expressions. Makes it clear to the programmer and the code will be more readable and easy to understand. 
    • Avoid performing read/modification access in a volatile-type variable more than once in a full expression or between sequence points. Makes it clear that the code is not compiler-dependent. 

]]

rule.name: R14_X_Control_Statement_Expressions
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

When using floating as a for loop counter, errors can occur involving floating point rounding, causing the program to work incorrectly and causing misunderstandings on the part of the programmer. 
In the case of the 3 expressions of the for loop, these must be directly related to the loop counter and the loop counter must not be modified in the for body. If these premises are broken, errors involving the number of repetitions of the for loop may occur. 
Regarding the rule 14.4, control expressions of if statements and loop statements must be essentially of boolean type, thus avoiding comparison failures (comparison of a pointer with NULL for example) thus preventing program functioning bugs. By following this rule, it is clear to the programmer that only true or false values are expected from this control expression. 

Cause

How does it happen

For 14.1: - Use a floting-point (float, double, long double) loop counter in loop statements; 
For 14.2:- When the first clause of the for statement do not define and initialize the loop counter- When the second and third clause objects are modified in the for statement loop body 
For 14.4:- When the controlling expressions of if, for, while, do while and switch statements are invariant (always true or always false) 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Avoid using floating variables in loop counters. Use larger type variables to perform more iterations rather than using a floating point variable. 
    • Be careful not to modify the loop counter in the loop body, causing the program to malfunction. 
    • In a control expression, avoid using compound expressions that provide multiple outputs. Use boolean essential type instead. 

]]

rule.name: R15_01_to_03_Goto_Usage_Constraints
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

Code legibility and, therefore, its maintenance are hard with the generalized used of goto. 

Cause

How does it happen

Using goto to control software flow. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • goto should not be used, unless on some specific situations. 
    • When using goto, perform forward jumps, and only jumps from inner to outer scopes (or same level scopes). 

]]

rule.name: R15_04_Iteration_Single_Exit_Point
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

The overuse of break or goto statements in loops make the code hard to read and maintain. 

Cause

How does it happen

Some algorithms can benefit, in terms of code reuse, to have multiple loop exit points. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Although it can have a benefit for code reuse, the usage of break or goto statements in loops should be reduced or non-existent. 
    • Thus, the algorithm should be reworked in order to guarantee more legibility and to have, at most, one exit point by loop, using a break or goto statement. 

]]

rule.name: R15_05_Function_Single_Exit_Point
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

The overuse of multiple return statements make the code hard to maintain and debug. 

Cause

How does it happen

To simplify the algorithms structures programmers choose to return early from functions. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • While returning early in some situations might have a small speed improvement, the recommendation is that the algorithm is written in a way that each function includes a single return statement, in the last line of the function. 

]]

rule.name: R15_06_Statement_Body_Shall_Be_Compound
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

The lack of compound statements may lead a developer to misinterpret the code. 

Cause

How does it happen

When developers don't use compound statements, they can wrongly interpret a bunch of badly indented statements as been the same block, but they don´t. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Always to use compound bodies for iteration or selection statements, even if the body has only one statement. 

]]

rule.name: R15_07_If_Else_If_Constructs_Not_Ending_With_Else
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

Default behavior or unforeseen circumstances are not covered if we do not have an else closing an if followed by an else if construct. 

Cause

How does it happen

Not closing an else if statement after an if statement. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Always close if statements followed by else if statements with an else, even if it has only a comment or a single semicolon. 

]]

rule.name: R16_X_Switches
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

The C standard allows a diverse panoply of switch/case configurations. While they are valid, they have two main drawbacks: 
- undefined behavior in some situations like having case clauses that are not direct child of a switch statement;- code that is difficult to read, like having a default clause in the middle of the switch statement;- code that is prone to errors, like having some clauses without a break statement. 

Cause

How does it happen

The use of code that does not follow these guidelines. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Rewrite the code in order to make it easier to maintain and less susceptible to errors, taking into consideration the rules described. 

]]

rule.name: R17_01_StdArg_Shall_Not_Be_Used
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

The use of variable number of parameters in functions have a high number of undefined behavior situations. In this sense, the best approach to minimize the risk is not using this feature. 

Cause

How does it happen

The write of functions that receive a variable number of arguments (like the built-in function printf), using the functions va_start, va_end and similar. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • The programmer should find an alternative solution, either creating different functions accordingly with the number of arguments, or receiving arrays of data. 

]]

rule.name: R17_02_No_Recursion
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

The use of recursion can easily raise stack overflow problems that are not easy to debug/detect. 

Cause

How does it happen

While writing recursive functions is an elegant approach to some problems, that should be avoided. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Alternative iterative solutions should be used. 

]]

rule.name: R17_03_Function_Shall_Not_Be_Declared_Implicitly
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

The use of a function without its prior declaration is valid in C, but this usage is dangerous because it can cause incorrect operation of the program. It may result in passing wrong arguments to function or assign incorrect return value. 

Cause

How does it happen

When a function is called without explicit declaration before. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Be sure to declare the function before using it. In this way it is possible to guarantee that the number of arguments and the return type are correct. 

]]

rule.name: R17_04_Non_Void_Has_Valid_Return
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

The C standard does not state what value shall be returned when the expression is omitted. 

Cause

How does it happen

The use of return without an expression. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Programmers should be sure to add a valid expression to every non-void return statement. 

]]

rule.name: R17_05_to_06_Functions_With_Array_Parameter
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

When passing array to a function, the size of the array needs to match the function prototype to avoid undefined behavior. When the parameter array of the function prototype has a fixed size, it makes it clear to the programmer that this size must be respected, thus avoiding unnecessary checks in the function body and code malfunctions. 
The use of static between [ ] (in the size of an array parameter) can cause misunderstandings on the part of the programmer, making him believe in a false sense of security since the compiler will issue a warning when out of size arrays were passed as parameter. 

Cause

How does it happen

Rule 17.5: 
- When passing array to a function that the size of the array does not match the function prototype. 
Rule 17.6 
- When static keyword is used in the size of an array parameter of the function. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Avoid passing arrays as a parameter when the size does not match the function prototype. 
    • Even if the size of the array in the function prototype does not have a fixed size, prefer to always make the size explicit so as not to cause interpretation errors and code malfunctions. 
    • Do not use static keyword between [ ] in the size of an array parameter of the function. For some compiler/processor combinations, the benefit of generating efficient code when using static does not outweigh the cost. 

]]

rule.name: R17_07_Value_Returned_By_Non_Void_Function_Shall_Be_Used
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

It is possible to call a non-void function and not use its return value. This behavior is quite common on the part of programmers, but it can hide several errors during program execution. 
By not using the return value, it can be difficult to check if the function call has an expected value or was successfully executed without the need for test routines, thus using more program resources and inducing the programmer to error. 

Cause

How does it happen

For rule 17.7: 
- Call a non-void function and not use its return value. This rule is valid both for individual calls in the body of functions, and for function calls in statements (if, else if, case, while, for) 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Avoid calling non-void function without assigning the result to a return variable. It makes it clear to the programmer that this value is necessary and can be used to validate the function itself. 

]]

rule.name: R17_08_Function_Parameter_Should_Not_Be_Modified
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

In C language, it is allowed that the function parameters are modified in the core, but they can cause misinterpretation by the programmer and failures in the execution of a function, believing that the effects of the modification of the parameters will be felt in the calling function. 

Cause

How does it happen

For rule 17.8: 
- Update/modify the value of parameters in the body of the function. This behavior should be applied when using side effects (prefix/postfix increment and decrement). 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Avoid modifying function parameters inside of the body of the function. 
    • Always create a copy of the parameter to an automatic object and modify that copy. 

]]

rule.name: R18_04_Pointer_Arithmetic
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

Pointer arithmetic is useful but poses a difficult mechanism to properly validate.It is also more prone to errors of invalid access to memory areas. 

Cause

How does it happen

The addition or subtraction of values to pointers may cause invalid memory access.The only exception is increment/decrement of pointers or the subtraction between two pointers. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Replace the pointer arithmetic by array subscripts. 

]]

rule.name: R18_05_Pointer_Nesting
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

The use of more than two levels of pointers make the code difficult to read and susceptible of errors. 

Cause

How does it happen

Declaration of variables with more than two levels of pointers. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Create the adequate structures to store the data without this level of indirection. Prefer multidimensional arrays over pointers. 

]]

rule.name: R18_06_Automatic_Storage_Addresses_Shall_Not_Be_Copied
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

Use of indeterminate address may lead to undefined behavior. 

Cause

How does it happen

The address of an automatic storage object becomes indeterminate when the object lifetime ceases. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Do not copy an automatic storage object address to another object that has greater lifetime. 

]]

rule.name: R18_07_to_08_Variable_Length_And_Flexible_Arrays
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

When using flexible arrays or with variable sizes in the code, this can imply in modifying the behavior of the sizeof operator, causing misunderstandings problems on the part of the programmer and failures in the execution of the program. 
Assigning values to variable or flexible array members can also be problematic, as they do not have a predefined size or, when they do, are not explicit to the programmer. 

Cause

How does it happen

Rule 18.7: 
- When declaring a flexible array in the code. 
Rule 17.6 
- When a variable-length array is declared in the code. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Avoid using flexible arrays or variable-length arrays in the code. 
    • Prefer to always make the size explicit so as not to cause interpretation errors and code malfunctions. 

]]

rule.name: R19_X_Overlapping_Storage
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

Rule 19.1: When an object is assigned to an overlapping object, it will cause unexpected behavior and/or program execution failures. In most cases, the object that has been overlapped will show inconsistent data. Any expression that have overlapping in the source code must be removed. 
Rule 19.2 The use of unions to access an object may result in problems, such as reading incorrect values or undefined behavior. An undefined behavior will occur when attempting to read a union member different than the one that the latest write operation was performed on. 

Cause

How does it happen

Rule 19.1: 
Overlapping in assign expressions between two different objects. 
Rule 19.2: 
When the union keyword is used in declarations. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Avoid using union keyword in declarations. Makes it clear to the programmer that is possible to read/write access to any member of the structure without problems. 
    • By avoiding using union, you also avoid overlapping issues that are covered by Rule 19.1. 

]]

rule.name: R20_01_Include_Directive_Precedence
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

If any code is placed before __#include__ directives, it's bad to readability, and may lead to program undefined behaviour. 

Cause

How does it happen

For example, if any _C Standard Library_ function is called before the respective _header_ file, may lead to undefined behaviour. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Only preprocessor directives and comments may precede __#include__ directives. 

]]

rule.name: R20_02_Invalid_Include_Names
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

Any occurrence of these characters or sequence of characters in the names of include directives results in undefined behavior. 

Cause

How does it happen

The C standard has no explicit restriction on using these peculiar name options. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Avoid these characters and character sequences at all costs when naming any file that will be included by a translation unit, especially since they may cause conflicts depending on the operating system or the platform building the codebase. 

]]

rule.name: R20_03_Includes_In_Wrong_Format
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

If the include directive does not follow those formats it is undefined behavior. 

Cause

How does it happen

For example, this rule applies after macro replacement, thus if a macro is defined as the name of file to be included but without the double quotes, when we try to include it, it leads to undefined behavior. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Always use double quotes surrounding the names of the files in the include directives and if they are a system header file use instead. 

]]

rule.name: R20_04_Macros_With_Keyword_Name
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

Defining macros with C keywords produces confusion and may cause undefined behavior on external file inclusions. 

Cause

How does it happen

There is a #define C Pre-Processor directive that overrides the name of a C Standard Keyword. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Use another name for the macro, trying to reduce possible name confusion. 

]]

rule.name: R20_05_Undef_Shall_Not_Be_Used
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

When using this directive, misinterpretation problems by the programmer can occur, since it is not clear whether the macros used at various points in the code are defined or not. 

Cause

How does it happen

When the #undef directive is used in the code to remove specific macro definition. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Do not use #undef directive in the code. This will avoid problems when an #undef undefines a macro that was defined in another file, as well as for a #undef directive that tries to undefine a non-existent macro. 

]]

rule.name: R20_10_to_12_Preprocessor_Concatenation_Operations
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

Multiple #, multiple ##, or a combination of the two preprocessor operators have no defined sequence in which they should be evaluated. As a result, the outcome of macro expansion is unpredictable. 

Cause

How does it happen

The # and ## are used to, respectively, turn the argument it precedes into a quoted string and to combine both sides of the operator into a single token, when a macro is expanded. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • The usage of these operators is discouraged. 

]]

rule.name: R20_13_Valid_PreProcessor_Directives
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

Any typo in a C Pre-Processor directive can prevent a whole file from being compiled. 

Cause

How does it happen

Either the directive is a typo or it is a non standard directive. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Non-standard C PreProcessor directives shall be avoided. 

]]

rule.name: R20_14_Preprocessor_IF_Else_In_Same_File
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

The usage described above not just makes it harder to understand and debug, but also prone to errors. 

Cause

How does it happen

Lack of proper code structure. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Reorganize your files in order to keep the C pre-processor conditional directives in a single file. 

]]

rule.name: R21_01_to_12_Usage_of_C_Standard_Library
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

- Rules 21.1 and 21.2 state that the programmer shall not redefine any word that is part of the Standard C Library, either as a function, type, variable or #define. This first restriction main risk is the redefinition of a known function or type from the Standard Library as being of other type or with other functionality, and therefore confusing other programmers that are expecting the default Standard C Library behavior. It also forbids names starting with an underscore.- Rules 21.3 to 21.12 state that some parts of the C Standard Library shall not be used. This second restriction is added given the set of undefined behaviors that some parts of the C Standard Library include. Note that 21.21 is a partial duplicate of 21.8. 

Cause

How does it happen

The redefinition of a function, type, variable or #define with a reserved keyword from the Standard C Library, or the usage of a forbidden method/variable/constant from some parts of the Standard C Library. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Do not use reserved names as identifiers, or identifiers starting with an underscore. 
    • Be aware of the Standard C Library problematic methods, and use either compliant libraries or other implementation approaches. 

]]

rule.name: R21_13_to_20_C_Standard_Library_Types
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

The use of some of the C Standard Library methods with specific types may lead to unspecified behaviors. 

Cause

How does it happen

- Values passed to any method shall be an integer in the range [-1, 255]- Pointers passed to memcpy, memmove or memcmp shall point to compatible types- Pointers passed to memcmp should point to integers, Booleans or enumerations only- The size_t value passed to any function shall not be larger than the size of the smaller string- The returned pointers from localeconv, getenv, setlocale or strerror shall be used as if they point to const types 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Taking into account the different causes, use typecasting or define variables in the correct type and check value ranges. 

]]

rule.name: R22_X_Resources
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

The following rules from series 22nd state issues that issues may lead to unexpected/undefined behavior:1. The resource acquired dynamically using functions from the Standard Library must be explicitly disposed;2. A memory block may only be released if it was allocated using a Standard Library function;3. The same file cannot be open for both read and write access on separate streams at the same time;4. Any attempt to write to a stream that has been opened as read-only is prohibited;5. A pointer to a FILE object shall not be dereferenced;6. After a stream has been closed, the reference to the FILE must not be used.7. Only the unaltered return value from any Standard Library function that can return EOF should be used when comparing the macro EOF;8. Before calling an errno-setting-function, the value of errno must be set to zero;9. After invoking an errno-setting-function, the value of errno must be compared to 0;10. Only when the last function called was an errno-setting-function should the value of errno be verified. 

Cause

How does it happen

- The C standard leaves the question of what would happen if someone tried to write to a read-only stream.- The address of a FILE object used to control a stream may be meaningful, therefore a copy of the object might not behave the same, according to the C standard.- The lack of use, inappropriate use, or misuse of _errno_ built-in variable. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • If it is intended to read and write to the same stream, or vice-versa, one should close the stream before opening it again with different permissions and performing any operations. 
    • Do not perform copies of a _FILE_ object or dereference it. Instead, any manipulation should happen to address. 
    • To avoid issues regarding the "_errno_ setting function", always: 
    • Set the value of _errno_ to zero before the function call; 
    • Test the value of _errno_ against zero after the function call; 
    • Only test the value of _errno_ against zero after an "_errno_ setting function"; 

]]

rule.name: DB_Parameter_Tampering
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

A malicious user could access other users’ personal information, by simply altering the reference parameter sent to the server. Thus, the malicious user could bypass access controls and access unauthorized records, such as other users accounts, stealing confidential or restricted information. 

Cause

How does it happen

The application accesses user information without filtering by user ID. For example, it may provide information solely by a submitted account ID. The application uses the user input to filter specific records from database tables, which contain sensitive personal information (e.g. user accounts or payment details). Since the application does not filter the records according to any user identifier, nor constrain it to a pre-computed list of acceptable values, a malicious user can easily modify the submitted reference identifier, and thus access unauthorized records. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Generic Guidance:  
    • Enforce authorization checks before providing any access to sensitive data, including the specific object reference.  
    • Explicitly block access to any unauthorized data, especially to other users’ data. 
    • If possible, avoid allowing the user to request arbitrary data by simply sending a record ID. For example, instead of having the user send an account ID, the application should look up the account ID for the current authenticated user session. 
    • Specific Mitigation: 
    • Filter the database query according to a user-specific identifier, such as the customer number.  
    • Map the user input to an indirect reference, e.g. via a prepared list of allowable values. 

]]

rule.name: Dangerous_Functions
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

Use of dangerous functions may expose varying risks associated with each particular function, with potential impact of improper usage of these functions varying significantly. The presence of such functions indicates a flaw in code maintenance policies and adherence to secure coding practices, in a way that has allowed introducing known dangerous code into the application. 

Cause

How does it happen

A dangerous function has been identified within the code. Functions are often deemed dangerous to use for numerous reasons, as there are different sets of vulnerabilities associated with usage of such functions. For example, some string copy and concatenation functions are vulnerable to Buffer Overflow, Memory Disclosure, Denial of Service and more. Use of these functions is not recommended. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Deploy a secure and recommended alternative to any functions that were identified as dangerous. 
    • If no secure alternative is found, conduct further researching and testing to identify whether current usage successfully sanitizes and verifies values, and thus successfully avoids the use-cases for whom the function is indeed dangerous 
    • Conduct a periodical review of methods that are in use, to ensure that all external libraries and built-in functions are up-to-date and whose use has not been excluded from best secure coding practices. 

]]

rule.name: Divide_By_Zero
rule.description:
![CDATA[

Risk

What might happen

When a program divides a number by zero, an exception will be raised. If this exception is not handled by the application, unexpected results may occur, including crashing the application. This can be considered a DoS (Denial of Service) attack, if an external user has control of the value of the denominator or can cause this error to occur. 

Cause

How does it happen

The program receives an unexpected value, and uses it for division without filtering, validation, or verifying that the value is not zero. The application does not explicitly handle this error or prevent division by zero from occuring. 

General Recommendations

How to avoid it

    • Before dividing by an unknown value, validate the number and explicitly ensure it does not evaluate to zero.  
    • Validate all untrusted input from all sources, in particular verifying that it is not zero before dividing with it.
